base_method_text.title:
Learning Motion Blur Robust Vision Transformers with Dynamic Early Exit
  for Real-Time UAV Tracking
base_method_text.summary:
Recently, the surge in the adoption of single-stream architectures utilizing
pre-trained ViT backbones represents a promising advancement in the field of
generic visual tracking. By integrating feature extraction and fusion into a
cohesive framework, these architectures offer improved performance, efficiency,
and robustness. However, there has been limited exploration into optimizing
these frameworks for UAV tracking. In this paper, we boost the efficiency of
this framework by tailoring it into an adaptive computation framework that
dynamically exits Transformer blocks for real-time UAV tracking. The motivation
behind this is that tracking tasks with fewer challenges can be adequately
addressed using low-level feature representations. Simpler tasks can often be
handled with less demanding, lower-level features. This approach allows the
model use computational resources more efficiently by focusing on complex tasks
and conserving resources for easier ones. Another significant enhancement
introduced in this paper is the improved effectiveness of ViTs in handling
motion blur, a common issue in UAV tracking caused by the fast movements of
either the UAV, the tracked objects, or both. This is achieved by acquiring
motion blur robust representations through enforcing invariance in the feature
representation of the target with respect to simulated motion blur. The
proposed approach is dubbed BDTrack. Extensive experiments conducted on five
tracking benchmarks validate the effectiveness and versatility of our approach,
establishing it as a cutting-edge solution in real-time UAV tracking. Code is
released at: https://github.com/wuyou3474/BDTrack.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces BDTrack, an efficient and motion blur robust tracking framework for real-time UAV tracking. It proposes a Dynamic Early Exit Module (DEEM) to streamline Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures and learns motion blur robust ViTs by enforcing invariance in feature representation against simulated motion blur. BDTrack integrates these components seamlessly, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple UAV tracking benchmarks.
base_method_text.methodology: The methodology involves two key components: (1) a Dynamic Early Exit Module (DEEM) that adaptively streamlines ViT architectures by dynamically exiting Transformer blocks based on an exiting score and a block sparsity loss, and (2) learning motion blur robust ViTs (MBRV) by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the feature representation of the original target template and its blurred version, using a linear motion blur simulation. The framework employs a single-stream approach with a ViT-based backbone and a prediction head.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The proposed method was evaluated on five UAV tracking benchmarks: UAV123, UAV123@10fps, VisDrone2018, UAVDT, and DTB70. The experiments compared BDTrack with 23 lightweight SOTA trackers and 12 SOTA deep trackers. Ablation studies were conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed components (MBRV and DEEM) and to analyze the impact of different parameter settings. Real-world tests were performed on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier.
base_method_text.limitations: The paper does not explicitly state limitations. However, potential limitations may include the reliance on simulated motion blur for training, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world motion blur. The effectiveness of the dynamic early exiting strategy might be sensitive to the choice of threshold and sparsity loss parameters. Additionally, while the method achieves real-time performance, its computational cost might still be a constraint for highly resource-limited UAVs.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions could include exploring more sophisticated motion blur simulation techniques, investigating adaptive thresholding strategies for dynamic early exiting, and extending the framework to handle other challenges in UAV tracking, such as occlusion and illumination variations. Applying the proposed techniques to other vision tasks beyond tracking could also be explored.
